arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Jeffrey Fisher argued that officers should know the law. He stated that citizens rely on this presumption.
North Carolina’s advocate argued that the Fourth Amendment allows reasonable errors. He emphasized that police do not need to be perfect.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests whether a police officer’s reasonable mistake of law can justify a traffic stop. North Carolina claims the officer acted reasonably. The driver claims the stop was unlawful.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: North Carolina wants the Court to uphold the traffic stop. It argues the officer’s reasonable mistake of law justifies the seizure.
The driver wants the Court to suppress evidence from the stop. It argues a reasonable mistake of law does not justify a seizure.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: North Carolina argues that the Fourth Amendment does not require police officers to be perfect. It claims reasonable mistakes of law should be tolerated.
The driver argues that officers must know the law. It claims a reasonable mistake of law does not provide probable cause for a stop.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts asked if the Fourth Amendment protects only against unreasonable searches. He questioned the basis for the stop.
Justice Alito asked if an officer could request a search after issuing a warning. He explored the scope of the interaction.
